The first lesson lasted forty minutes, and covered roughly forty feet. Each time I let the clutch out, the truck lurched, shuddered, and died. Delia did not say anything. She reached over, turned the key, and waits for me to try again.

The trick, she finally explained, is that the clutch and the gas are not two pedals, they are one conversation. One foot lets go while the other presses down, and the engine tells you, through the seat and the steering wheel, whether you have it right. Neither my aunt nor my cousins was able to explain it any better than that, and I suspect nobody can.

By the second week I could get the truck moving on flat ground. Hills were another matter. The road up to the barn climbs to a gate that has to be opened by hand, which meant stopping on a slope and starting again once more without rolling back into the ditch. Stalled halfway up the hill for the third time, the gate looked impossibly far away. Delia walked down, leaned on the door, and told me the one thing that finally helped: stop listening to the engine and start listening to the truck. It’s the same sound, she admitted, but it means something different once you stop being afraid of it.

I got my license that fall, in my mother’s sedan, which is an automatic. I have not driven a stick shift in years. But when I pull away from a stoplight, there is still a small part of my left leg that attains for a pedal that isn’t there.

title: The Choir on Level Three
text:
Every Thursday at seven, about thirty people climb the stairwell of the parking garage on Harlan Street to the third level, which is empty once the shops close. They bring folding chairs, a pitch pipe, and thermoses of tea. For an hour and a half, they sing.

The choir’s founder, a retired music teacher named Odette Farris, chose the garage for its sound. Built for cars rather than voices, the choir found the garage surprisingly generous. Concrete is hard and flat, and it reflects nearly everything that strikes it. A single voice in the middle of level three bounces between the floor and the ceiling so many times that it seems to hang in the air after the singer stops. Farris calls this effect “free harmony”: every note you sing is still sounding when you sing the next one. Churches built of stone produce the same effect, which is partly why so much early choral music was written for them.

The echo has a cost. Fast passages blur, because each new note arrives before the last one has faded. Consonants, the sounds that make words understandable, turns to mush. Farris chooses the music accordingly slow hymns, rounds, and chords held for eight or ten beats. Nobody sings anything quick.

Not everyone in the building is a fan. The night attendant, Luis Ybarra, spent the choirs first month asking them to leave, the garage, he pointed out, was for cars. He has since changed his mind. He now keeps the ramp barrier raised on Thursdays so that latecomers who arrive after the start can walk up, and on two occasions he has sung the bass line of a round from inside his booth.

Last spring the city asked whether the choir would consider moving to a community center. The members voted to stay. A garage — Farris says, is the only room in town that nobody has tried at making pretty, so nobody has ever made it quiet either. Carpet, curtains, and seats that are upholstered swallow sound; bare concrete gives it back.

title: Why the Bus Is Yellow
text:
Before 1939, a child in the United States might ride to school in almost anything. Some districts used converted delivery trucks; others used farm wagons with benches bolted to the bed. The vehicles came in whatever color the seller happened to have, and a bus in one county looked nothing as a bus in the next.

The person who changed this was Frank Cyr a professor of rural education at Columbia University. Cyr has spent a year surveying how children in rural districts got to school. Finding conditions that alarmed him. Buses varied in size, in safety, and how they were built, and a driver approaching one on a country road had no way of recognizing it as a vehicle full of children.

In 1939 Cyr invited transportation officials from every state to a week-long conference in New York. The group, which included engineers, paint experts, and school administrators, were asked to agree on standards that any manufacturer could follow. They settled dozens of questions about size, construction, and signaling equipment. The most famous decision, though, was the color.

The delegates pinned strips of paint in dozens of shades to a wall and argued. They wanted a color that would stand out against almost any landscape and also in addition in the half-light of early morning, when many children were waiting at the roadside. They also wanted black lettering to be easy to read against it. The winner was a deep yellow with a slight orange tint. Its since been known by various names, but the shade itself has changed remarkably little.

Part of the color’s success is that it became a symptom. Drivers learned, over decades, that a vehicle of that particular yellow might stop suddenly and let children out. The color works less because yellow is uniquely visible than because everyone knows what it means. A school bus painted blue would be just as easy to see, however, it would be far harder to understand.

title: The Ferry at Halloran’s Landing
text:
For ninety-one years, the only way across the Merrin River between Oakford and the county seat was a flat wooden ferry pulled along a steel cable. It held four cars, or two cars and a hay wagon, and in good weather the crossing took about six minutes. Its two diesel engines was replaced only once, in 1958. The ferry moved steady, and nobody seemed to mind.

The last operator, Delia Marsh, ran the ferry from 1994 until the day it closed. She was in charge with everything on board: the engines, the cable, the tickets, and the patience of the passengers. Marsh’s brother owned a hardware store in the county seat for many years. The ferry — officially Ferry No. 3, never had a name painted on its hull, but everyone in Oakford called it the Halloran.

The cable that pulled the ferry, was replaced every ten years. Each new cable was to heavy for a crew to lift, so it arrived on a flatbed truck and was unrolled by a winch. The ferry lost their cable twice in floods, in 1973 and again in 2003, and both times the landing washed out. Rebuilt twice, Oakford residents never thought of the landing as permanent.

Marsh kept a logbook. Every crossing went into it the time, the number of vehicles, and the height of the river on the gauge by the landing. The logbooks now fill eleven shelves, they are the only complete record of traffic on that stretch of road. The records of every crossing are kept in the county library, where a historian from the state university has begun to read them.

When the new bridge opens in the fall of 2019, the ferry made its last crossing the same week. The bridge takes forty seconds to cross. Therefore, people in Oakford still drive down to the old landing on summer evenings, just to look at the water. Marsh goes too. She says the ferry ran every single day without fail, daily, for ninety-one years, and she would rather remember that than the bridge.

title: What the Glacier Says
text:
Erin Sato studies glaciers by listening to them. Her main instrument is a hydrophone, an underwater microphone about the size of a soda can, which she lowers into the fjords of southeast Alaska on a weighted line. The glaciers that she studies all end in the sea. What she hears there is not silence. Glacial ice is full of air bubbles that were trapped when the snow first fell, some of them hundreds of years ago. As the ice melts, each of the bubbles burst with a small crack, and where a glacier meets the sea, the cracks add up to a steady crackling roar, louder than rain on a roof.

Sato first noticed the roar in 2009, the year she initially heard it, while recording harbor seals for another project. The seal’s calls kept disappearing under a hiss that she assumed was a fault in her equipment. Which it was not. The hiss was the glacier.

Since then, Sato learned to read the sound. Warm ocean water reaching the face of a glacier excels the melting, so the fjords where that water arrives are the loudest. Sediment in the water muffles the sound; a fjord clouded with silt can seem quieter than it is. Neither the tides nor the temperature of the water explains all of the change from one week to the next. Sato is as interested in the quiet fjords than in the loud ones.

Sato shared her recordings with a physicist, Grace Obi, and she built a model. The model links the loudness of the roar to three things: the temperature of the water, how fast the ice is moving, and the number of bubbles in each liter of ice. The roar is a rough measure of melting, however, it cannot tell anyone exactly how much ice is being lost.

Satellites can measure how much a glacier has shrunk over a year. For example, they cannot see through cloud, and southeast Alaska is under cloud most of the time. Sato’s goal is modest: a cheap way to watch glaciers that no satellite can see. Her hydrophones — which cost about as much as a used bicycle, are cheap enough to lose, and she loses several every summer.

title: The Shallow End
text:
I learned to swim the summer I turned thirty. For most of my life I had arranged things so that the question never came up or arose. I sat at the edge at pool parties, I volunteered to watch the bags at the beach, and I choosing hotels by whether they had a gym rather than a pool. Nobody noticed, or, if they noticed nobody said anything. By thirty I had become an expert at a skill nobody knew I needed: looking relaxed near water.

The class met at seven in the morning at the municipal pool on Garfield Street. The pool had been built in 1962 with money from a local bond. There were six of us in the class, all adults, and we was all embarrassed. Our instructor — a retired lifeguard named Pearl Oduya, did not waste time on reassurance. Her first lesson had nothing to do with swimming. It was about breathing. We stood in the shallow end, put our faces in the water, and breathe out through our noses until the bubbles stopped.

This was harder than it sounds. The body does not want to breathe out underwater; every instinct says to hold on at whatever air it has. Pearl said that holding your breath is what makes people panic, because the lungs fill with stale air and the brain reads the pressure as an emergency. Breathing out, she said, is how you ensure your body that you are not drowning. Taking me four mornings to believe her.

The floating came next, and it was worse. Holding one hand under the small of my back, I was told by Pearl to lie still, look at the ceiling, and let the water hold me up. Each time she took her hand away, I sank — not because I was too heavy but because I tensed every muscle I had. As far as Pearl was concerned, the trick was to do nothing, and doing nothing turned out to be the hardest thing I have ever tried to learn.

One morning in the third week, I lay back perfect still and looked at the ceiling. After a while I noticed that Pearls hand was gone. Nobody clapped, which I appreciated. I don’t know how long I had been floating on my own. The other five, who had been practicing at the far wall, was watching.

I am not a strong swimmer now. I can manage four lengths of the pool before I need to rest, and my stroke would not impress anyone. Therefore, I go in the deep end without checking where the ladder is, and last August, at a friend’s lake cabin, I swam out to the raft with everyone else instead of guarding the towels. The raft had lost it’s ladder years ago, so I climbed up the side.

title: Playing to the Picture
text:
When the Crescent Theater shows a silent film, the music does not come from a speaker. It comes from Hollis Mayberry who sits at an upright piano just below the left edge of the screen and plays for the entire length of the picture, sometimes for more than two hours without a break. He has done this about eleven hundred times.

Silent films were never meant for being watched in silence. In the 1920s, even a small-town theater employs at least a pianist. The grand movie palace’s in large cities kept full orchestras. In fact, there was more musicians working in movie theaters than in concert halls. Studios sometimes sent out cue sheets. Lists of suggested pieces keyed to the scenes. As a result, most accompanists ignored them and improvised. Very little of that music was written down, so almost none of it survives.

Mayberry improvises too. Before a screening, he watches each film several times. Pen in hand, the scene changes get marked in a small notebook. He also notes which characters need a theme of their own. On the night, though, he does not read music. He watches the screen and plays what the screen seems to ask for: a rolling figure in the bass for a train, a thin, high melody for a letter being read, and for the moment before a kiss, nothing at all.

That last choice is the one audiences ask about most. Silence, Mayberry says, is louder then any chord a pianist can play, and it only works if it is rare. A film that has music under every frame teaches it’s audience to stop hearing it. A film where the music stops once, at the right moment, makes three hundred people hold their breath at the same time.

The job’s three hazards — the length of the films, the hard piano stool, and the light from the screen — have never changed. The last is the worst, flickering blues and grays fall across the keys and make it hard to see his own hands. Once, during a Buster Keaton comedy, a string in the middle register snapped, and he played the last forty minutes around the gap.

Younger musicians occasionally asks Mayberry to teach them. He tells each of they to start by watching films with the sound off and humming along. Most of them expect a method, and he does not have one. What he has is eleven hundred evenings of watching faces on a screen and deciding, a second before they change, what they are about to feel.

title: The Lichen Clock
text:
On a boulder high in the mountains of Norway, a pale green crust the size of a coin may be older than most cathedrals. It is a lichen, Rhizocarpon geographicum and it grows so slowly that geologists have learned to use it as a clock. The method, called lichenometry, was developed in the 1950s by an Austrian botanist named Roland Beschel, who noticed that the largest lichens on a surface seemed to say something about how long the surface had been exposed. Beschel also played the cello in an amateur orchestra.

The principal behind it is simple. When a glacier retreats or a rockfall exposes fresh stone, the surface started bare. Within a few decades the first lichens arrive on the wind, take hold, and they begin to spread outward in a rough circle. Because the growth is slow and fairly steady, the diameter of the largest lichen on a surface gives an estimate of how long ago that surface was uncovered in the past.

To turn a diameter into a date, a researcher needs a growth curve. This is built from surfaces whose ages are already known, such as: gravestones, bridges, old walls, and moraines dated by other means. However, a lichen on a gravestone carved in 1850 cannot be older than the stone, so its size sets a limit on how fast lichens in that region grow. Enough of these surfaces, measured carefully and when they are dated precisely, produce a curve that can be applied to rocks with no written record at all.

The method has obvious weaknesses. Growth rates vary with climate, so a curve built in one valley cannot simply be carried to the next. Like a tree ring, geologists read the lichen’s diameter as a record of time, and like a tree ring it can be misread. The largest lichen on a boulder may have been damaged, or two lichens may have grown together and look like one. Some researchers now measure dozens of the largest lichens on each surface. Rather than trusting a single one.

For example, lichenometry reaches where other methods struggle. Radiocarbon dating is indecisive for the last few centuries, and tree rings are useless above the tree line. For the moraines left by glaciers during the Little Ice Age, which ended in the nineteenth century — a tape measure and a patient eye can sometimes give an answer that no laboratory can.

title: The Radio Hour at Saint Brigid’s
text:
In 1951, a retired schoolteacher named Agnes Folau pursued the board of Saint Brigid’s Hospital to let her wire a small speaker beside every bed on the children’s ward. The agreement between she and the board was simple: the program could run as long as it cost the hospital nothing. Folau paid for the wire herself borrowed a microphone from a church, and began broadcasting from a supply closet — the only room the hospital could spare.

The program ran for one hour each evening. Folau read stories, played records, and announcing birthdays. On Fridays she took requests. Written in pencil on scraps of paper, the nurses brought the requests down the hall to her closet. Anyone could send one, and she always read out the name of whoever had asked. The children could not see her, and most of them never met her, so many remembered her voice for the rest of their lives.

The idea spread. By the end of the decade, volunteers are running similar programs in more than forty hospitals across the region. Most of them started by people who had heard about Saint Brigid’s from a friend. The equipment was cheap and the rules were few; no advertising, no news that might frighten a patient, and programs never running past lights-out.

Hospital radio reached its peak in the 1970s, when some stations broadcast over the clock and trained their volunteers in interviewing and sound engineering. It declined for a simple reason television. Once every bed had a set of its own, and later a telephone that could stream anything, a volunteer reading a story over a crackling speaker could not compete.

A few stations survive, however, most closed long ago. The one at Saint Brigid’s closed in 1998, but the supply closet is still there, and the hole in the wall where Folau ran her first wire has never been plastered over. A small card beside it gives her name and the date. Nurses who have worked on the ward for years say that parents stop to read it more often than the children do.

title: The Ice Harvest
text:
Before the electric refrigerator, ice was a crop. Every winter, farmers in New England — and across much of the northern United States, cut ice from frozen ponds in blocks. They packed the blocks in sawdust, stacked them in windowless icehouses, and then they would open the doors in summer. Most of that ice stayed close to home and did not travel far. A family might keep a small icehouse behind the barn, and a town might fill a larger one for it’s butcher and its doctor.

The man who turned ice into an export was Frederic Tudor a Boston merchant, whose friends considered the idea a joke. In 1806 he ships a cargo of pond ice to the Caribbean island of Martinique. Much of it melted on the voyage, the rest melted on the dock, because nobody on the island had anywhere to store it. Tudor lost money on that trip and on several after it, and his partners withdrew and left the debts to him alone. He spent time in debtors’ prison.

What he learned from those failures was that selling ice meant selling the habit to use it. Each of the ports he shipped to got an insulated icehouse of its own, and he taught bartenders to chill drinks. He also offered ice free. Until customers came to expect it. By the 1830s his ships were carrying ice as far as India. A voyage of four months. Even so, a surprising share of the cargo arrived frozen.

The harvest itself was hard, cold work. First, horses pulling a plow fitted with steel blades that scored the ice into a grid. Men with long saws finished the cuts. The blocks, each weighing a hundred pounds or more, was floated down a channel to the icehouse and pushed up a ramp. A thaw at the wrong moment could totally trash a season’s crop in a day.

The trade peaked near the end of the nineteenth century, when millions of tons were cut each winter. Similarly, it collapsed. Able to run in any season, mechanical ice plants could make ice anywhere, without depending on the weather. Home refrigerators finished the job: within a generation, the icebox was an antique. Today the old icehouses are mostly gone, though a few ponds are still cut by hand each winter, with the old saws, for visitors to watch.

title: Counting Stars from the Driveway
text:
On a clear night far from any town, a person with ordinary eyesight, can see a few thousand stars at once. In the middle of a large city, the same person might count a few dozen. The difference lays not in the sky but in the air above the city. That air scatters the light of streetlamp’s, signs, and windows back toward the ground. Astronomers call this glow skyglow, and it has been growing for more than a century. Astronomy is one of the oldest of the sciences.

The act of measuring it is harder than it sounds. Satellites can photograph cities from above, but they see light going up, not the glow a person sees looking up. Some satellites also blind to the bluish light of modern LED lamps. Nevertheless, for a picture of the sky as people actually experience it, researchers have turned to people.

Since 2006, a program called Globe at Night has asked volunteers to step outside, find a familiar constellation and, compare what they see with a set of charts. Each of the charts shows the constellation as it would appear under a different level of skyglow. The charts range from: a handful of bright stars to a crowded field. The volunteer picks the closest match and submitting it along with the time and place. No telescope is needed — just patience and about ten minutes for the eyes to adjust to the dark.

A single observation is not worth much. A volunteer may choose the wrong chart, or a thin cloud may hide the fainter stars, however, tens of thousands of observations begin to average out such mistakes. Analyzing more than fifty thousand of them in 2023, the sky was found by researchers to be brightening by nearly ten percent a year. It was far faster than satellite data had suggested. A sky that shows 250 stars when a child is born would show fewer than half as many by the time that child turns eighteen.

The cost is not born only by astronomers. Migrating birds navigate partly by the stars, and a sea turtle hatchlings’ first crawl is toward the brightest horizon, which should be the sea. Yet the remedy is unusually simple and not complicated. Light that is shielded, aimed downward, and turned off when nobody needs it do not reach the sky. Unlike most kinds of pollution, this one disappears the moment its source is switched off.

title: The Slide Rule’s Last Decade
text:
For more than three hundred years, anyone who needed to multiply large numbers quickly reaches for the same tool. The slide rule, a ruler with a second ruler sliding inside it — was marked with scales that grew more crowded toward one end. It was invented in England in the 1620s, shortly after John Napier published his work on logarithms and by the twentieth century it hung from the belt of nearly every engineer.

The idea behind it is elegant. Logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition, the kind a ruler can do with lengths. To multiply two numbers, the first number is lined up by a user on one scale with the start of the other, then reads the answer beneath the second number. The whole operation takes a few seconds of time.

The slide rule had limits that its users learned to live by. It gave answers to about three digits, which was enough to build a bridge but not for balancing a bank account. Also nothing about where the decimal point went. A reading of 42 might mean 4.2, 420, or 42,000; the user had to know which. Trained to expect this, engineers learned to estimate every answer in their heads before calculating it. Some of them say they never lost the habit.

Similarly, the end came quickly. In 1972 Hewlett-Packard released the HP-35, a calculator small enough to fit in a shirt pocket that could do everything a slide rule could, and it worked to ten digits. It cost $395, more than a weeks pay for a young engineer. Within a few years the price has fallen to a fraction of that. The major manufacturers of slide rules soon stopped making it. Keuffel & Esser, the best-known American maker, produced its last one in 1975 and gave it to the Smithsonian.

Slide rules has not disappeared entirely. Collectors buy them, repair them, and they display them in glass cases. There is still a few pilots who carry a circular version, called a flight computer, to work out fuel and wind. Apollo astronauts carried slide rules to the Moon as a backup. For most people, though, the slide rule is a puzzle found in a grandparent’s desk drawer: a ruler that does not seem to measure anything.

title: A Mind in Eight Arms
text:
In 2016, an octopus named Inky leaves his tank at the National Aquarium of New Zealand during the night. Arriving in the morning, the lid was found slightly open by staff, with a wet trail across the floor leading to a drain. The drain, which emptied into the sea. Inky was never seen again, and the people who ran the aquarium was more impressed than upset.

Stories like Inky’s have made octopuses famous as escape artists, but they also raze a serious question. The question is simple; how did an animal so unlike us become so smart? An octopus is a mollusk, closer to a clam than to any animal we usually think of as clever. Its ancestors and ours parted ways more than five hundred million years ago. Its brain owes nothing to ours, therefore, whatever intelligence it has evolved on its own.

That intelligence is organized very differently and in a different way from ours. An octopus has about five hundred million neurons, roughly as many as a dog, but two-thirds of them is in its arms rather than its head. Each arm can taste what it touches and reacting without waiting for instructions from the brain. Researchers have watched a severed arm reach for food and pass it toward where the mouth would have been.

In the laboratory, octopuses solve problems that were designated for mammals. They unscrew jar lids to reach a crab inside, learn to navigate simple mazes, and recognize individual keeper’s. Sometimes they squirt water at a keeper who they dislike. Also playing. Given a floating bottle, some octopuses will push it into the current of their tank again and again — behavior that looks like nothing so much as a child with a ball.

What puzzles biologists most is the short life span. Most octopuses live only a year or two and they rarely meet their parents. Few of them ever look after they’re young once the eggs have hatched. After all, intelligence is usually thought to pay off over a long life, spent learning from others. The octopus seems to have built a remarkable mind without either, and scientists are still trying to work out why.

title: The Well with Thirteen Floors
text:
In the dry country of western India, water has always been worth more then shade, and for centuries builders there found ways to provide both. The result was the stepwell — a well that a person does not lower a bucket into but walks down into. Instead of a narrow shaft, a stepwell is a wide pit lined with stairs, descending downward level by level to wherever the water happens to be.

The most dramatic example is Chand Baori, in the village of Abhaneri, which is more than a thousand years old. It’s thirteen levels drop about thirty meters, and its three stepped walls hold some 3,500 narrow steps arranged in a zigzag pattern. The fourth wall holds: a gallery of carved pavilions. Seen from the rim, the steps seem to shift and flicker, and photographs rarely make the depth believable. Visitors, who see it for the first time, often need a moment to understand what they are looking at.

Still, the design was more than a spectacle; it solved a practical problem. Rainfall in the region comes in a few months of monsoon, and the level of groundwater rise and fall by many meters over a year. A bucket on a rope works only if the rope is long enough, a staircase works at any depth. The logic was simple: in the wet season, people descended a few flights, and in the dry season, they kept going.

In contrast, stepwells were also social places. Because the air near the water stayed cooler than the air at the surface — often by several degrees, villagers gathered there in the hottest part of the day. They came to fetch water, to wash clothes, and resting in the cool. Women, who did most of the water carrying, met on the landings and talked. Many stepwells were decorated with carvings of gods and dancers, and some were built by wealthy women for public gifts.

Under British rule, many stepwells are closed or filled in. Officials considered the wells’ standing water unhealthy, and piped water and pumps made them seem unnecessary. Hundreds abandoned and left to fill with silt. In recent decades, some have been cleaned and restored, partly for tourists and partly for the reason that falling water tables have reminded planners why the wells were built in the first place.

title: Building the Grid
text:
The first crossword has appeared in a New York newspaper in December 1913. Its creator, a journalist named Arthur Wynne, called it a “word-cross.” It was shaped like a diamond — not a square. Wynne was born in Liverpool, England. Readers liking it enough to write letters asking for more. Within a decade, the puzzle had become a national craze, the first book ever published by Simon & Schuster, in 1924, was a collection of crosswords. It sold hundreds of thousands of copies to buyers.

Not everyone approved. Some newspapers dispelled the puzzle as a fad. They complained that it wasted readers’ time, and The New York Times held out for years. It finally began printing a Sunday crossword in 1942, shortly after the United States entered the Second World War, on the theory that readers facing grim news might welcome a distraction. The puzzle’s first editor there, Margaret Farrar, set many of the rules that American constructors still follow.

Those rules are stricter than most solvers realize. The pattern of black squares must look the same and identical when the grid is turned upside down. Every white square must belong to both an across word and to a down word, and no word may be shorter than three letters. The grid also has to connect, a solver must be able to travel from any white square to any other without crossing a black one.

Within those limits, the constructors real work is filling the grid. Constructors usually begin by a few long “theme” entries that share a joke or a hidden pattern, then fit shorter words around them. In practice, this is harder than it sounds. Working corner by corner, a single awkward spot can force the constructor to tear out half the puzzle and begin again. A fill that relies on obscure words, will frustrate solvers no matter how clever the theme is.

Today many constructors use software, it searches word lists for combinations that fit. The software is fast, but it cannot tell a lively word from a dull one, or a fair clue from an unfair one. Those judgments still belong to the guy running the show, and they are the reason one puzzle feels like a conversation while another feels like a test.

title: Mile Nineteen
text:
I signed up to volunteer at the city marathon because a friend needed one more person for her water station. I assume the job would take an hour. It took seven hours, and it taught me more about endurance than any race I have run.

Our station, at mile nineteen, had one job; to hand out water to anyone who wanted it. My friend who had worked the station for six years, showed me how to pinch a cup so that it would not splash. The race organizers had supplied us with four thousand paper cups, and we spent the first hour filling them in rows on folding tables. The leaders passed without slowing down. Behind them came the crowd, and for the next three hours my friend and me barely looked up.

The runners who reached us in the fourth hour were different, many had stopped running and were walking with a stiff, careful gait. Some had written their names on their shirts, and we shouted each runners name as he or she passed. One man, a retired mail carrier running his first marathon at seventy-one, asking me how far he had left. He nodded, finished his water, and walks on. Therefore, twenty minutes later, I realized I had never warned him about the long hill at mile twenty-two.

The last runners, were barely moving, but every one of them took a cup and thanked us. Paper cups were first used for drinking water in the early 1900s. I had expected the final hour to be dull, but it turned out to be the part I am most grateful at. The runners at the back had a different kind of race: they were not trying to win or even to finish in a good time, only to finish. They had trained less, worried more, and they were hurting more than anyone who had passed before them.

When the course closed, we stacked the tables and swept up the cups, it took nearly an hour. My legs ached, though I had not run a single step. I felt oddly prideful anyway. I never learned whether the mail carrier — a man whose name I did not know, finished the race.

title: The Sharpener’s Cart
text:
Every Saturday in summer, my grandfather pushed a wooden cart through the streets of our neighborhood and sharpened whatever people brought him; kitchen knives, garden shears, scissors, and, once, a sword. The cart had been built by his own father, and it was older than he was in age. A grinding wheel was mounted on top, and a foot pedal turns it.

I was eight the first summer he let me come along, and my job was the bell. Ringing it at every corner, the neighbors would come out with their knives wrapped in dish towels. Most of them, I soon learned, had been coming to my grandfather for years. He could tell, from one glance at the edge — who had been cutting bread and who had been prying open cans.

He taught me to hold the blade at a steady angle, to press lightly, and to let the wheel do the work. I never quite got the hang with the angle. A blade that is ground too hard grows hot and loses its temper. I found that amusing, since losing your temper was exactly what he told me never to do at the wheel. By noon, the neighbors’ knives were lined up along the cart, each one tagged with its owner’s name. He charged a quarter a knife, and everyone on the street was familiar to the price. He never argued on it, even when people offered less. Some people paid more than he asked, he always put the extra in a coffee can for my school shoes. Nevertheless, the can was usually full by the end of August.

The last summer I rode with him, the lesson he repeated most was: a dull knife is more dangerous than a sharp one, because it slips. He said that was true of tools — and of most other things as well. The cart itself, still stands in my parents’ garage. Its wheels are cracked and its paint has diminished, but the bell still works. Sometimes I take it out, to ring it once, and put it back.
